Pre-training on high-resolution X-ray

Xiao Wang1, Yuehang Li1, Wentao Wu2, Jiandong Jin2, Yao Rong1, Bo Jiang1*, Chuanfu Li3 and Jin Tang1
Abstract
Existing X-ray image based pre-trained vision models are typically trained on a relatively small-scale dataset (less than
500,000 samples) with limited resolution (e.g., 224 × 224). However, the key to the success of self-supervised
pre-training of large models lies in massive training data, and the maintenance of high-resolution X-ray images
contributes to eﬀective solutions for some challenging diseases. In this paper, we proposed a high-resolution
(1280 × 1280) X-ray image based pre-trained baseline model on our newly collected large-scale dataset containing
more than 1 million X-ray images. Our model employs the masked auto-encoder framework, wherein the tokens that
have been processed with a high rate are used as input, and the masked image patches are reconstructed by means
of the Transformer encoder-decoder network. More importantly, a novel context-aware masking strategy has been
introduced. This strategy utilizes the breast contour as a boundary for adaptive masking operations. We validate the
eﬀectiveness of our model through its application in two downstream tasks, namely X-ray report generation and
disease detection. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our pre-trained medical baseline model can achieve
comparable to, or even exceed, those of current state-of-the-art models on downstream benchmark datasets.
Keywords: High-resolution X-ray image, Pre-trained big models, Masked auto-encoder (MAE), Medical report
generation
1 Introduction
X-ray medical image analysis is one of the major important
research directions in smart healthcare. Common X-ray
applications include lesion segmentation [1], detection [2],
disease prediction [3], and medical report generation [4].
Previous works usually focused on a single task based on
pre-trained backbone networks on the ImageNet dataset
[5], which were deep convolutional neural networks, such
as VGG [6] and ResNet [7]. Early deep learning meth-
ods greatly accelerated the development of medical image
analysis but gradually reached their performance bottle-
neck. Potential reasons include privacy issues with medical
data leading to scarcity, experienced doctors being unable
to provide high-quality annotated data for various reasons,

Based on our observations, deliberations, and discus-

images and the standard resolution of pre-trained mod-

typically trained on standard image resolutions, such as
224 × 224, whereas actual X-ray image resolutions may
reach levels as high as 2000 × 3000. This discrepancy can
lead to a signiﬁcant loss of image information originally
present in high-resolution data when down-sampling oc-

are usually pre-trained on public datasets, such as MIMIC-

scale model pre-training. Considering the aforementioned
issues, the following questions are naturelly raised: “Can
we further expand the scale of X-ray images for the pre-
training task? Is it possible to conduct this pre-training
task at higher resolutions? Could more prior information
be leveraged to improve the eﬀectiveness of pre-training?”
In this paper, we answer these questions by proposing
a novel MAE framework that adopts the context-aware
masking strategy pre-trained on massive (approximately 1
million) high-resolution X-ray images. As shown in Fig. 1,
we resize the input X-ray image to 1280×1280 and believe
that the high-resolution images can better preserve the
detailed information of the original data. Then, we parti-
tion it into non-overlapping image patches and project the
patches into token representations. The input tokens are
dropped out with a high ratio (larger than 70%) by follow-
ing the MAE [14], however, we propose a novel context-
aware masking strategy instead of the random masking
used in the MAE. This is because chest X-ray images con-
tain prominent contour line information, and doctors typ-
ically are more concerned with information about lesions
in the chest area. The visible tokens are added with posi-
tional encodings. Then, we feed them into a Transformer
encoder. The masked tokens are randomly initialized and
concatenated with the output of the Transformer encoder

The contributions of this paper can be summarized as
follows:
1) To our best knowledge, we propose the ﬁrst pre-

2 Related works
In this section, we introduce the algorithms that are related
mostly to ours, including pre-training on medical images
and downstream tasks. More works can be found in the
following surveys [22–26].
2.1 Pre-training on medical image
Inspired by the success in natural language processing and
natural images [27], the pre-training techniques proposed
for the medical image analysis can be categorized into
two main streams, i.e., the contrastive learning based [16,
28–31] and masked token based reconstruction schemes
[19, 32, 33]. A brief summary of these models is provided
in Table 1. For the masked token based reconstruction
frameworks, the inputs are usually masked with a high
ratio and attempt to reconstruct them using an encoder-
decoder network. Speciﬁcally, Chen et al. [19] proposed
the M3AE which took the masked medical image and lan-
guage as the input and conducted feature-level fusion via
cross-attention. They proposed two independent decoders
for the reconstruction of visual and language modality.
Zhou et al. [33] introduced the masked record modeling
(MRM) framework which reconstructed masked image
patches and masked report tokens following a multi-task
scheme. Xiao et al. [20] pre-trained a foundation model
based on masked autoencoder [14] and conducted exten-
sive ablation studies on the advantages of the ViT on CNN.
For contrastive learning based models, the relation-
ships between medical images and reports are considered
mainly for pre-training. Speciﬁcally, GLoRIA proposed
by Huang et al. [28] is an attention-based framework for
learning global and local representations by contrasting
image sub-regions and words in the paired report. The
global to dense level representation learning (G2D) pro-
posed by Liu et al. [29] is a medical vision-language pre-
training framework that improves the granularity and pro-
vides more accurate grounding for the learned features.
Zhan et al. [30] proposed the UniDCP, which was a uniﬁed
model that supported multiple medical ﬁne-tuning tasks.
They designed cross-modal prompts to harmonize hetero-
geneous inputs from multiple pre-training tasks. Wang et
al. [31] proposed the PhenotypeCLIP, which also followed
the contrastive learning framework and learned more
ﬁne-grained phenotype-based representations to bridge
the gap between vision and language eﬃciently. CXR-
CLIP [38] ﬁrst generates image-text pairs from image-
label datasets via prompt engineering and conducts pre-
training via three kinds of contrastive loss. Unlike these
works which conduct pre-training on low-resolution X-
ray images or contrastive learning between X-ray and En-
glish text, we propose a pre-trained foundation model on
high-resolution X-ray images and support medical report
generation in both English and Chinese.

In this paper, we focus on handling two representative
tasks, including medical report generation [44–51] and
disease classiﬁcation [52–57]. For reporting generation,
Stephanie et al. proposed the MAIRA-1 [44] which com-
bined CXR-speciﬁc image encoder and ﬁne-tuned LLM

knowledge-driven encode, retrieve, paraphrase (KERP)
method. At its core is the proposed universal implemen-

images and sequences. ORGAN [47] is an observation-

3 Method
In this section, we ﬁrst provide an overview to help under-
stand our pre-training framework. Then, we explore the
details of pre-training on high-resolution X-ray images.
After that, we introduce the downstream tasks used to val-
idate the eﬀectiveness of our pre-trained model, including
Chinese/English report generation and disease prediction.
3.1 Overview
As illustrated in Fig. 1, our pre-training scheme follows the
masked auto-encoder framework [14] that attempts to re-
construct the highly masked input patches. Note that, we
take high-resolution X-ray images as the input to better
retain their raw detailed information. The image is parti-
tioned into non-overlapping regions and transformed into
token representations via a convolutional layer. Inspired by
the cue in the chest region may be more important than
other regions, we introduce a simple but eﬀective context-
aware masking strategy by masking more patches within
the chest regions. This helps the model to focus on these
regions in the pre-training phase. The visible tokens are
fed into the ViT encoder and the outputs are concate-
nated with the randomly initialized masked tokens. Then,
a Transformer decoder network is adopted to reconstruct
the input image. Once the pre-training is ﬁnished, we ﬁne-
tune the Transformer encoder for the downstream task to
achieve a higher performance. More details will be intro-
duced in the subsequent sections.
3.2 Pre-training stage
In this section, we focus on the details of our pre-training
from the perspective of input processing, context-aware
masking, transformer encoder and decoder, and loss func-
tion.
Input processing. Given the raw X-ray images, we ﬁrst re-
size them into a ﬁxed-resolution I ∈RH×W×1, where the
image height H and width W are both set to 1280. Fol-
lowing the Transformer encoder used in the MAE [14],
we partition the whole image into N non-overlapping re-
gions {P1,P2,...,PN}, and the resolution of each region is
64 × 64 × 1. Then, we adopt a convolution layer (kernel
size 64×64) to transform the image patches into the token
representations {X1,X2,...,XN} whose dimension is 1024.
After we obtain these tokens, the MAE framework masks
them with a high ratio, and the rest of them are treated
as visible tokens. For example, He et al. [14] masked 70%
of the tokens for the natural image, and Xiao et al. [20]
claimed that the best downstream performance could be
achieved when 90% of the tokens were removed in the pre-
training stage of their MAE-based X-ray model. However,
the above methods rarely consider the contextual informa-
tion of chest X-rays for the masking operation.
Context-aware masking. In this study, we propose a
context-aware masking strategy speciﬁcally designed for
the chest radiographs. We delineate a boundary to divide
the image into an outer and an inner region, with the inner
region masked at a higher probability to highlight the diag-
nostic importance of the thoracic region. Let X ∈RN×L×D
represent the input sequence of tokens, where N repre-
sents the batch size, L corresponds to the sequence length
(spatial dimensions of the ﬂattened image), and D indicates
the feature dimension of each token. We denote pouter and
pinner as the masking probabilities for the outer and inner
regions, respectively. The masking steps are as follows:

3.3 Downstream tasks
In this work, we validate our proposed framework by intro-
ducing the pre-trained transformer encoder (i.e., ViT-L)
into two downstream tasks, including X-ray image based
report generation and disease prediction, as illustrated in
Fig. 1 (b) and (c).
X-ray image based report generation. Given the X-ray
image, the task of report generation aims to describe the
disease information via natural language. Usually, this task
is formulated as English sentence generation. In addition,
we build a new X-ray dataset for Chinese report gener-
ation. More details about this dataset are introduced in
Sect. 4.1.2. In our implementation, we build our report
generator based on the R2Gen1 toolkit proposed in Ref.
[58].

Disease prediction. This task can be treated as a standard
multi-category classiﬁcation problem by mapping the in-
put X-ray image into a distribution of the response score of
each category. However, this approach may ignore the se-
mantic information of category names, which is also useful
for high-performance recognition. In this work, we follow
the VTB2 [59], which formulates the multi-label classiﬁ-
cation task as a vision-text fusion problem, for the disease
prediction. As shown in Fig. 1 (c), we adopt the pre-trained
ViT encoder to extract the features of the input X-ray im-
age and utilize the CLIP text encoder to embed the given
disease name. Then, we fuse the two modalities via a multi-
modal Transformer network and predict the disease via a
fully connected (FC) layer.
4 Experiments
In this section, we ﬁrst introduce the datasets, evaluation
metrics, and implementation details in Sects. 4.1, 4.2, and
4.3, respectively. Then, we focus on reporting and analyz-
ing the results of the medical report generation and disease
prediction, in Sects. 4.4 and 4.5. After that, we present ex-
tensive ablation studies of our model in Sect. 4.6 and vi-
sualize the reconstruction of the masked tokens, similar
matrices, generated medical reports, and disease predic-
tions in Sect. 4.7. Additionally, we describe the limitations
of this work in Sect. 4.8.
4.1 Datasets
4.1.1 Pre-training dataset
To pre-train a high-performance X-ray foundation model,
the ﬁrst step is the collection of large-scale X-ray images.
Therefore, a large-scale and high-resolution dataset that

4.2 Evaluation metrics
For the X-ray report generation task, we adopt the widely
used four metrics for the evaluation, including captions
generated by diverse experts (CIDEr) [62], bilingual eval-
uation understudy-4 (BLEU-4) [63], recall-oriented un-
derstudy for gisting evaluation - longest common sub-
sequence (ROUGE-L) [64], and metric for evaluation of
translation with explicit ordering (METEOR) [65]. Specif-
ically, CIDEr measures the consensus between the gener-
ated captions and multiple reference captions. It evaluates
the quality of image captioning by computing the cosine
similarity between n-grams in the generated caption and
those in the reference captions. BLEU-4 evaluates the qual-
ity of machine-generated translations or text summaries
by comparing them with reference translations or sum-
maries. It measures the precision of n-grams (usually up
to 4-grams) in the generated text compared with the ref-
erence texts. ROUGE-L assesses the quality of text sum-
maries or translations by comparing them with reference
texts. It focuses on the longest common subsequences be-
tween the generated and reference texts, emphasizing re-
call. METEOR evaluates machine-generated translations

recall, as well as the alignment between the generated and
reference texts. It also incorporates stemming and syn-

For the disease prediction task, the area under the re-
ceiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), F1, and
accuracy metrics are adopted to compare the performance
of diﬀerent models. Speciﬁcally, AUROC is a metric com-
monly used to evaluate binary classiﬁcation models. It
measures the ability of the model to distinguish between
positive and negative samples across diﬀerent decision
thresholds. The F1 score is the harmonic mean of preci-
sion and recall. It is commonly used in binary classiﬁcation
tasks to provide a single metric that balances both preci-
sion and recall. Accuracy simply measures the proportion
of correctly classiﬁed instances out of the total number of
instances evaluated.
4.3 Implementation details
Pre-training stage. In the pre-training phase, we resize the
X-ray image to a ﬁxed resolution, i.e., 1280 × 1280. The
learning rate is set as 0.000,25, and the weight decay is 0.04.
The batch size is 1024 and a total of 83 epochs are trained
on our dataset. The AdamW [66] is adopted as the opti-
mizer. The pre-training is conducted on a server with eight
NVIDIA A800 GPUs (80 GB) and about 660 h are needed
for our pre-training phase.
Downstream tasks. For the generation of Chinese med-
ical reports, we ﬁne-tune the model using our PCC X-ray
dataset, which comprises a total of 200,000 X-ray images.
The training conﬁguration is as follows: we resize the im-
ages to 224×224, set the batch size to 16, employ RoBERTa
[67] as the tokenizer, and conduct training over 60 epochs.
In the case of English medical report generation, we ﬁne-
tune the model on the IU-Xray dataset. Before inputting
the images into the model, we resize them to 384 × 384.
We set the batch size to 16, establish a maximum sequence
length of 30, and keep other parameters identical to those
of R2Gen [58].
For the disease prediction task, we performed experi-
ments on the RSNA-Pneumonia dataset via code derived
from the visual-textual baseline (VTB). We conﬁgured the
batch size to 200 and set the input image size to 224×224,
while leaving the remaining conﬁgurations unchanged.

This work attempts to conduct self-supervised pre-
training based on MAE on a high-resolution X-ray dataset
and validates it on two mainstream medical downstream
tasks. The results indicate that our X-ray image based

4.9 More details about our dataset
Our dataset, which is unparalleled in scale and quality,
consists of over 1 million high-resolution X-ray images
with a resolution of approximately 2000 × 3000, ensuring
the richness and diversity of the data sourced from multi-
ple hospitals. We have meticulously annotated more than
20,000 X-ray images in Chinese, leveraging the expertise of
professional doctors and PhD. students from the First Af-

to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the annotations.
However, we acknowledge potential biases in the dataset,

5 Conclusion and future work
In this work, we summarize the issues of existing X-
ray image-based pre-training methods and propose pre-
training a high-resolution baseline model. Speciﬁcally,
we employ the self-supervised pre-training framework of
masked auto-encoder and design a new context-aware
masking strategy. For the downstream tasks, we test our
model on both English/Chinese report generation and dis-
ease prediction. The experiments on several benchmark
datasets fully validate the eﬀectiveness of our model.
In future work, we aim to address several key challenges
and explore new directions to further enhance the capabil-
ities of our X-ray image-based pre-training method.
1) The X-ray baseline model proposed in this paper is
based on Transformer but has a complexity of O(N2), re-
sulting in high memory consumption and computational
cost when handling high-resolution X-ray data. In the fu-
ture, we attempt to introduce new lightweight network ar-
chitectures such as state space model/Mamba [79] to ad-
dress the computational complexity issues. 2) While self-
supervised visual pre-training has shown promising re-
sults, there is still room for improvement in terms of over-
all accuracy. To enhance the model’s representation abil-
ity, we will explore multi-modal pre-training approaches.
These approaches involve the integration of large language
models and knowledge graphs to extract semantic infor-
mation from text and graph-based data. We expect that
this will facilitate the model’s comprehension of the con-
text of medical images and improve its performance in
downstream tasks. 3) To further improve the performance
of our model in tasks such as medical report generation,
we intend to introduce additional cues and prompts. In ad-
dition, we will explore the integration of other prompting
techniques, such as instruction tuning, to guide the model
toward more speciﬁc and relevant outputs.
There are a number of potential issues in the context
of these challenges: 1) Integrating new network architec-
tures into the existing pre-training framework may require
signiﬁcant customization to ensure compatibility and per-
formance. 2) Eﬀective fusion of multi-modal data sources
requires the development of new algorithms to align and
integrate information from diﬀerent domains. 3) Experi-
ments with more complex models and larger datasets re-
quire signiﬁcant computational resources that need to be
managed eﬃciently.
By addressing these directions and challenges, we aim to
make signiﬁcant advances in X-ray image analysis and its
applications in medical diagnostics.

Abstract: Existing X-ray image based pre-trained vision models are typically trained on a relatively small-scale dataset (less than 500,000 samples) with limited resolution (e.g., 224 × 224). However, the key to the success of self-supervised pre-training of large models lies in massive training data, and the maintenance of high-resolution X-ray images contributes to eﬀective solutions for some challenging diseases. In this paper, we proposed a high-resolution (1280 × 1280) X-ray image based pre-trained baseline model on our newly collected large-scale dataset containing more than 1 million X-ray images. Our model employs the masked auto-encoder framework, wherein the tokens that have been processed with a high rate are used as input, and the masked image patches are reconstructed by means of the Transformer encoder-decoder network. More importantly, a novel context-aware masking strategy has been introduced. This strategy utilizes the breast contour as a boundary for adaptive masking operations. We validate the eﬀectiveness of our model through its application in two downstream tasks, namely X-ray report generation and disease detection. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our pre-trained medical baseline model can achieve comparable to, or even exceed, those of current state-of-the-art models on downstream benchmark datasets.
